sentences.pattern: People may move not because + single reason, but because + combined pressures or opportunities.
sentences.cn: 人们迁移可能并非由于单一原因，而是多种压力或机会共同作用。
sentences.example: People may move not because wages are low alone, but because secure work and training are unavailable.

sentences.pattern: When + qualification or experience + is not recognised, migrants who + expertise + may have to + lower-level outcome.
sentences.cn: 当某种资历或经验得不到认可时，拥有相关专长的移民可能不得不接受较低层级的结果。
sentences.example: When overseas qualifications are not recognised, migrants who have medical expertise may have to take unrelated jobs.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Qualification recognition can turn migration into productive employment.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Host countries waste valuable skills when overseas credentials are assessed slowly or inconsistently.
writingIdeas.argument: A nurse who cannot obtain local recognition may work in a job that uses none of her clinical training, even while hospitals lack staff. Automatic acceptance is not always safe because professional standards differ. However, transparent assessments and short bridging courses can identify genuine gaps without requiring an experienced worker to repeat an entire education. This comparison between verified competence and job placement is more useful than judging people by where a certificate was issued. Better recognition would improve migrants’ incomes and help employers fill urgent vacancies.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Integration policy should include established residents as well as newcomers.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Community trust is more likely to grow when migration-related investment addresses shared local pressures.
writingIdeas.argument: Rapid population growth can increase demand for housing, schools and clinics in particular districts. If new services are described as benefits exclusively for migrants, established residents may feel that their own needs are being overlooked. Expanding a clinic for everyone, while adding interpretation where needed, solves the practical pressure without dividing users into rival groups. Shared sports projects and neighbourhood associations can create contact that abstract campaigns rarely achieve. Integration is therefore strongest when public policy improves participation and capacity across the host community.

speaking.question: Describe someone you know who moved to a new place.
speaking.answer: A close friend moved from a small inland town to a coastal city for her first professional job. She knew nobody there and initially found everyday tasks, such as choosing a neighbourhood and understanding the bus network, surprisingly tiring. She joined a weekend running group, which gave her regular contact with people outside work, and after a few months she began to feel settled. I admired the way she remained curious rather than constantly comparing the city with home. She still calls her family several times a week and visits when possible. Her experience showed me that moving is not one dramatic decision; it involves many small adjustments before a place feels familiar.

speaking.question: What helps newcomers integrate into a community?
speaking.answer: Language ability matters, but opportunities to use the language in meaningful situations matter just as much. Stable housing and fair access to employment give people the security to build relationships. Local institutions can help by explaining services clearly and organising activities around shared interests rather than nationality alone. Established residents also influence integration through ordinary behaviour: an invitation, a helpful explanation or patience with an accent can make a real difference. Newcomers should learn local expectations, but integration cannot reasonably be treated as their responsibility only.

reading.title: When Qualifications Do Not Travel
paragraphs: On arriving in a new country, an experienced civil engineer found work inspecting goods in a warehouse. His degree was genuine, his former employer supplied references, and local construction firms were recruiting. What he lacked was a familiar professional record: regulators could not easily compare his university modules, safety training and project responsibilities with domestic requirements.

This problem, often described as “brain waste”, differs from a simple skills mismatch. The expertise exists in the destination country but remains unused because evidence about it does not pass smoothly between institutions. Employers, who may be unable to judge an unfamiliar college, tend to prefer local experience; professional bodies must protect safety; and migrants cannot acquire domestic experience until someone hires them. The result is a circular barrier that language training alone cannot remove.

A provincial pilot programme replaced a single document check with several forms of evidence. Applicants submitted portfolios, completed practical simulations and, where a specific gap was identified, attended a short course. Participants entered work related to their previous professions more often than a comparison group using the conventional route, although researchers cautioned that volunteers for the pilot may have been especially motivated.

The process was neither quick nor cheap. Simulations required trained assessors, and small occupations could not offer enough candidates to run them frequently. Yet the programme also revealed that some apparent shortages were failures of recognition rather than failures of supply. It did not lower professional standards: an applicant unable to demonstrate essential knowledge still needed further study.

Qualifications are not objects that can simply be carried across a border unchanged; they are claims interpreted by employers, regulators and educational systems. More reliable interpretation will not place every migrant in an ideal job. It can, however, distinguish a genuine training gap from an administrative one—and prevent a society from searching overseas for skills already present within its own workforce.

questions.prompt: Choose the best heading for Paragraph B.
questions.answer: A circular barrier to skilled employment
questions.explanation: The paragraph shows how unfamiliar credentials, local-experience demands and hiring depend on one another.

questions.prompt: Every participant in the pilot found work related to a previous profession.
questions.explanation: The passage says participants entered related work more often, not that every participant did so.

questions.prompt: What did the pilot reveal about some skills shortages?
questions.explanation: The final sections say some shortages reflected failed recognition rather than absent skills.
options: They were caused entirely by language ability.
They existed only in small occupations.
Relevant skills were already available locally.
